What a unique experience!! @mcsorleysoldalehouse is NYC’s oldest continuously operating saloon since 1854. Even Abe Lincoln came here! It’s simple, you either get “light beer” or “dark beer”. Don’t ask what brand, what size, nothing. You get two at a time and that equals a pint. Something I loved about this place was all the photos on the walls representing what this bar looked like back in the days. It was so easy to pick out all the photo locations as it has barely changed! And the waiters wear sports coats which was a nice touch, making them easy to point out. Be sure to bring cash only to this first come, first serve bar and enjoy some brews!

📍McSorley’s Old Ale House - 15 E 7th St - New York, NY

McSorley’s Old Ale House is a historic Irish pub that opened in Manhattan, New York in 1854. It was founded by Irish immigrant John McSorley. He arrived in New York City in 1851 during the Irish Potato Famine. Three years later he opened an ale house on East 7th Street which he named “The Old House at Home”. It wasn’t until 1908 when the pub was renamed “McSorley’s Old Time Ale House” (the word “time” was later dropped). John passed away in 1910 and his son Bill took over the pub. After it passed through a couple more owners, night manager Matthew Maher bought the pub in 1977. Maher would continue to run McSorley’s until he passed away in 2020. It is now run by his daughter Teresa and her husband Gregory. McSorley’s is recognized as the oldest Irish Pub in New York City.

As the name would imply, McSorley’s Old Ale House strictly serves beer and no other alcoholic beverages. They only serve two kinds of ale: light or dark… that’s it. Both are brewed by Pabst Brewing Company. Several notable figures visited the pub over the years, including President Abraham Lincoln who visited in 1860 after his famous speech at nearby Cooper Union. Magician Harry Houdini performed a handcuff-escaping trick at the pub in the early 1900s. He escaped from his own cuffs (which are still hung from the ceiling) as well as a policeman’s cuffs (which are still cuffed to the bar). McSorley’s was also infamous for not allowing female patrons inside long after other bars began to do so. The first woman didn’t set foot inside the pub until 1970.

I recently visited McSorely’s while I was in the Village to see a concert. I grabbed a spot at the bar and ordered a round of both the Irish Pale Ale and the Irish Black Lager. I enjoyed them with a delicious cheddar cheese plate. It’s worth noting that it’s CASH ONLY here. While there’s nothing particularly special about the food or drink at McSorely’s, you’re getting a big slice of history and the fellowships of a plethora of pub regulars. There’s a reason why McSorely’s has lasted so long; it’s a New York City institution! 🍻🇮🇪

When I realized I had dinner and lunch plans in the city on consecutive days, I had an idea…maybe I could just stay overnight in a hotel by myself. I instantly felt guilty and almost talked myself out of it, but I forced myself to at least suggest it to Rob, and he was on board. He would just have to relieve the babysitter that night, and then do the morning routine the next day on his own. Even though I do so much solo on a regular basis, I felt bad asking him to give me this break. But, the truth is, being pregnant with a toddler is really hard…both physically and mentally. What I needed more than anything was time to myself when I didn’t have to think about my to-do list or other people’s needs, when I could (mostly) turn off mom mode and give my brain a break. Honestly, it makes me a little mad that my first inclination was guilt, and I’m sure I’m not the only mom who has trouble prioritizing herself. But, I’m here to say that it’s okay to do something for you, it’s not selfish, and it doesn’t mean you love your kid(s) any less 💕 

I stayed at the super chic @thewallacehotel on the UWS. Shoutout to the sweet lady at the front desk who upgraded my room when I told her why I was there. All I did was eat queso in a bathrobe, then put on my PJs and read in bed, but it was glorious!

How do you celebrate the life of a truly rare spirit & special friend who left too soon, who was the epitome of great character, generosity, who drew people together in all parts of her life, professionally, personally with so many groups of friends & colleagues that she kept close, supported, advocated for and went above & beyond touching their lives & the lives of their loved ones!  An amazing Celebration of Life followed by an after celebration at the iconic Dive Elegance Bar in the East Village “The Holiday Cocktail Lounge” where rockers, poets, intellectuals, revolutionaries gathered for nearly 100 years.  We miss you everyday Jo! “But we pay tribute to you amongst the amazing memories of you and notable historical company - 1990’s- The Ramones and The Bouncing Souls, who immortalized it in their “Holiday Cocktail Lounge” song. In the 1980s, Madonna, Iggy Pop and Keith Richards frequented its bar stools. Poets Allen Ginsburg and W.H. Auden were regulars in the 1970s, as was Godlis, who documented the punk rock scene, Frank Sinatra and Shelly Winters made it their haunt in the 1960s. Holiday Cocktail Lounge opened in 1950, succeeding The Ali Baba Burlesque, which entertained guests in the 1940s. The venue began its libational history back in 1919 as a speakeasy hidden in Ann’s Beauty Shop, attracting the likes of Russian revolutionary Leon Trotsky during his East Village sojourn. It was the city’s 50th licensed bar when Prohibition ended in 1933. The building itself dates back to 1835.” You will live on in my heart & inspire me to continually live everyday with carpe diem! Our first “luxury” hotel stay — and what we didn’t expect.

My friend and I splurged on The Knickerbocker in NYC — our first high-end hotel, with big hopes for comfort and care. Instead, our first night left us anxious and uneasy.

A bellman offered to “help,” asked to put his number in my phone, then connected me with an unverified “driver” charging $75 one-way. Not a hotel service.
That same night, the concierge snapped when I asked what could be done for a woman begging with her baby outside. She told me CPS would make the mom spiral into jail, depression, drugs — and the baby would end up “in danger in the hands of strangers.” Then she told me to “just enjoy [my] vacation.”

The extra $60/night “premium view” was scaffolding. Towels we hung to reuse were removed. Even basic kindness felt transactional, with tip expectations everywhere.

The manager empathized but defended staff as “top performers,” saying the concierge was “from here.” When I shared I’d found a real outreach program for that mom and baby, she brushed it off — more worried about my review than what had happened.

Luxury? Not without humanity.

There’s this trend going around the wellness space right now where practitioners list “10 things they no longer do” — everything from fluoride toothpaste to receipt paper to eating cake. And I get it. I get what they’re trying to do… but let’s be real: this is just another flavor of fear-mongering and gaslighting.

Women are already carrying the weight of chronic illness, exhaustion, people-pleasing, trauma, and shame spirals. The last thing we need is more rules, more “don’ts,” and more reasons to believe we’re failing.

Because here’s the truth: the fear of eating that slice of cake is 1,000x worse for your body than the cake itself. The panic of reading every single label, obsessing over toothpaste, or trying to live in a hazmat bubble is what actually keeps your nervous system locked in survival mode. And when your body doesn’t feel safe, it won’t release symptoms. It won’t regulate. It won’t heal.

Healing doesn’t happen through obsession. It happens through safety. Through joy. Through a nervous system that finally trusts you. That’s why my work isn’t about shaming women into perfection, but about helping them rewire their nervous system, release fear loops, and finally feel safe in their own body again.

This is what actually changes everything.

Wow, it’s only been 9 months since we opened Bánh Anh Em, yet it feels like so much longer.

Earlier this year, we were still trying to figure out how to even open the doors. We faced so many issues with construction, and had to switch to another company with no clear timeline for when we would open. 

At the same time, we were short-staffed at our Bánh UWS location, so I was working nonstop during the day and doing R&D at night. The night before opening, I panicked. We had run out of time. I texted our staff without much hope that anyone would show up.

But after 11pm, one by one, everyone came — after a long day working at Bánh. They helped us get the store ready for the next day’s big moment: building chairs, scrubbing kitchen walls, figuring out how to make the bánh ướt towers not slip. They went home, slept only a few hours, and then came back early to be ready to open our doors.

Bánh Anh Em was truly built by all of the anh em here with their dedication. This has always been, and will always be, a complete team effort.

At the time, we didn’t think about anything else. We just hoped people would come and try our food.

Thank you so much for your pouring love and support since day one.

This work reflects on the experience of people with pending asylum applications. After filing a claim, it can take weeks, months, years, or even more than a decade to receive an interview that determines whether the case is approved or moved to court.
